narrative: The model estimated a 52% chance that you will leave your job, so it treated leaving as slightly more likely than staying and denied the promotion. This is not a judgment of your ability; it reflects retention risk in the information available. The strongest signal was that you reported having other job opportunities. That is uncommon among employees predicted to stay—only about one in four had outside opportunities—and it pushed the prediction most strongly toward leaving. The second signal, your six to ten years in your current organization, worked in the opposite direction and was the main reason the model still saw meaningful retention. In contrast, your eleven-plus years of overall experience pushed toward leaving; very few employees predicted to stay had that much total experience, so it suggested a profile that may be ready to move. Your master’s degree, medical-sector role, and low salary band may add to this picture, but they were less influential than the three signals above. Before reconsidering promotion, the organization should discuss your career path and concrete internal opportunities, review whether your pay and rewards match your effort, and clarify what promotion readiness would require. You should ask for specific feedback on the gap between current performance and the next role, and whether retention concerns can be addressed through a development plan rather than denying advancement.
